title: Wyoming Voters Oust GOP Faction that Wants to Crack Down on Elections
author: Daniel Nichanian
content:
It’s an unusual sight in the Trump-era GOP: In many of Wyoming’s state
primaries last week, Republican voters chose candidates who defended the
state’s voting systems and election workers, over those who amplified the
president’s lies about voter fraud.

In the contest to be Wyoming’s next chief elections official, GOP voters
nominated a county commissioner, Robert Short, who says elections are secure
and that reforms should focus on making voting more accessible and inclusive.

And they ousted many of the Republican lawmakers who, in recent legislative
sessions, pushed hard to restrict voter access and crack down on
[everything](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/02/09/election-reform-a-top-
freedom-caucus-priority-the-house-just-killed-a-lot-of-it) from mail ballots
to voter registration.

The results are sure to shake up the balance of power in Wyoming and deflate
the far-right’s ambitions to make this state a laboratory of MAGA-style
election administration. Marguerite Herman, who lobbied against those proposed
restrictions at the legislature on behalf of the League of Women Voters of
Wyoming, told _Bolts_ she was delighted to see that many of the officials who
championed them won’t be in office come next year.

“We’re hoping we don’t have to fight those battles yet again, and fight all
the false bases for it,” she said. “We’re hoping we never have to face these
restrictive things to answer security issues that don’t exist.”

The state’s ultra-conservative faction did get a victory in Wyoming’s marquee
federal primary, as Chuck Gray, the outgoing secretary of state and chief
proponent of new voter restrictions, won a crowded primary for the U.S. House
seat with 25 percent of the vote.

Assuming he prevails in November, Gray would be able to champion severe
changes to federal election law from D.C., most notably President Trump’s
[SAVE Act](https://www.lwv.org/blog/what-save-act-means-2026-midterms-
approach), which would require voters nationally to provide proof of
citizenship to register. But his agenda suffered multiple setbacks in
Cheyenne.

Gray [won the state’s previous](https://boltsmag.org/wyoming-first-election-
denier-secretary-of-state/) secretary of state race in 2022 as an election
denier who said the 2020 presidential election was “clearly rigged.” Over the
next four years, he worked with far-right lawmakers in Wyoming’s powerful
Freedom Caucus, which has run the state House since 2024 but remained a
minority in the state Senate, to push a barrage of restrictive election bills,
animated by unfounded claims of rampant voter fraud.

This ultraconservative bloc had successes, notably a [harsh
law](https://boltsmag.org/wyoming-voter-registration-proof-of-citizenship-
law/) that took effect last year that requires voters to provide proof of
citizenship to register to vote. Wyoming’s governor
[criticized](https://sos.wyo.gov/Elections/Legislation/2025/Chp172_HB156_HEA57_Proof-
of-Voter-Residency-Registration-Qualifications_wGovernor-No-Sign-Letter.pdf)
the legislation and said it threatened to disenfranchise eligible voters, but
he still let it become law without his signature.

But many of the far right’s core proposals stumbled, [including
bills](https://wyofile.com/gray-wyoming-freedom-caucus-back-trump-plans-to-
ban-mail-in-ballots-voting-machines/) to ban electronic voting machines and
ballot drop boxes, a secure voting method that has fueled baseless conspiracy
theories about the 2020 election. During his 2022 campaign, Gray [hosted
screenings](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2022/06/15/sos-candidate-chuck-gray-
hosts-screenings-of-2000-mules-movie/) of the
[debunked](https://www.reuters.com/article/factcheck-usa-mules/fact-check-
does-2000-mules-provide-evidence-of-voter-fraud-in-the-2020-u-s-presidential-
election-idUSL2N2XJ0OQ/) film “2000 Mules,” which falsely blamed drop boxes
for Trump’s loss in the presidential race.

![](https://boltsmag.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/08/26030749726586-scaled.jpg)Wyoming Secretary of State
Chuck Gray speaks with a reporter during the National Associate of Secretaries
of State Conference in Washington on Jan. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Cliff Owen)

Heading into Aug. 18, the Freedom Caucus hoped to expand its power in Wyoming,
a ruby red state where GOP primaries largely determine which ideological
factions hold power. Had they succeeded, they may have been able to push
through their elusive demands.

Instead, the primaries largely [turned into a
rout](https://wyofile.com/wyoming-freedom-caucus-faces-loss-of-at-
least-9-incumbent-lawmakers/) for Freedom Caucus members.

In the primary for secretary of state, Freedom Caucus Chair Rachel Williams
lost by 13 percentage points to Short, a Converse County commissioner who took
the opposite approach as Gray and the Freedom Caucus as he ran on defending
elections as trustworthy.

“Methods utilized for conducting elections in Wyoming by county clerks are
incredibly effective at finding issues,” he said in an interview with _Bolts_
after his primary win.

“We should not be making it harder for legitimate citizens to vote,” he said.

Short says he opposes the policy demands of Gray and his legislative allies,
including the proposals to ban electronic voting machines and eliminate drop
boxes. He stressed that mail ballots and drop boxes are a critical convenience
in Wyoming, where many people live very far from population centers.

“Many of these folks work on very remote jobs, whether it be in the extraction
industry or in agriculture, meaning that they do not have the luxury of just
going to town to vote whenever they feel like it,” he said. “For them being
able to drop their ballot into a box, that is the most effective way to allow
them to cast their vote.”

Instead, Short says he wants to find ways to expand voter access, like
allowing people to register to vote online; Wyoming is
[currently](https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/online-voter-
registration) one of only eight states that do not allow online voter
registration.

He also would like to set up voting opportunities within assisted-living
facilities. “I believe this would go a long way in helping these folks who
spent most of their lives as voting members of our society and now are having
challenges voting simply because of their living situation,” he said.

Short also said he’d be open to bringing automatic voter registration to
Wyoming, a practice that exists in nearly half of U.S. states and that’s
[meant to shift the burden](https://boltsmag.org/automatic-voter-registration-
medicaid-oregon-colorado/) of registering from citizens to public
[agencies](https://boltsmag.org/michigan-automatic-voter-registration-prison/)
that already possess information to determine which residents are eligible.
“Whatever we can do to make voter registration and access to the ballot easier
for Wyoming citizens, I am absolutely in favor of,” he said.

But when asked about the proof-of-citizenship law that passed last year, Short
did not offer a definitive answer, instead mirroring Governor Mark Gordon’s
qualified criticism that it’s important to restrict voting to only citizens,
but that the law risks keeping some people from voting. “I was not in
opposition of the premise, but the practice is challenging for some folks,” he
said.

Alongside Short’s victory in the secretary of state primary, voters tossed out
many of the far-right lawmakers who were in charge of their faction’s voting
agenda.

Of the eight Republicans who sit on the Wyoming House Corporations, Elections,
and Political Subdivisions Committee, the panel that reviews election bills
and that has been the incubator of restrictive voting proposals, seven lost
their primaries last week.

All seven were members of the Freedom Caucus or aligned with it, [according to
_WyoFile_](https://wyofile.com/in-stunning-upset-wyoming-freedom-caucus-loses-
most-of-its-house-seats-backslides-in-senate/).

Many other Freedom Caucus members not on the Corporations Committee also lost
their GOP primaries last week, and the Caucus will no longer control a
majority of the state House as it did since 2024.

Christopher Dresang, the Republican who
[ousted](https://oilcity.news/community/elections/2026/08/18/2026-primary-
election-republican-dresang-ousts-locke-in-wyoming-house-district-35/)
Corporations Committee member Tony Locke in the 35th House District, confirmed
in an exchange with _Bolts_ that he differs on election issues from the man he
beat, as he rejected the very premise that there’s any problem to address.

Dresang said he opposes banning drop boxes and mandating pen-to-paper
ballots—changes Locke has supported. And in a clear break with Gray and the
Freedom Caucus, he repeatedly said he would follow the lead of local election
officials when it comes to voting procedures.

“I trust county clerks and local election officials, who run these elections
and answer to their own voters, over one-size-fits-all mandates from
Cheyenne,” he said. “They’re the ones administering these elections and best
positioned to judge what's secure and workable for their county.”

Short, too, praised election workers on the [campaign
trail](https://county17.com/2026/03/04/converse-county-commissioner-robert-
short-enters-secretary-of-state-race/)—and again in an interview with _Bolts_.

“Election workers, election judges, county clerks—they are our friends,
neighbors, our family members; they are volunteers, most of them,” he said.
“To insinuate that they would do this job for nefarious reasons is really
disingenuous. It’s insulting.”

The language is a stark break from Trump’s usual rhetoric, as well as that of
Gray and his allies, who have continually
[warred](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/01/22/gray-county-clerks-accuse-
each-other-of-gaslighting-over-ballot-drop-boxes/) with county clerks and
their statewide association. The president of the County Clerk’s Association
of Wyoming, who did not reply questions for this story,
[often](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2025/02/06/bills-to-ban-voting-machines-
killed-in-committee/) [testified](https://www.wyomingpublicmedia.org/politics-
government/2025-01-30/hand-counting-votes-ban-on-ballot-drop-boxes-election-
bills-move-through-legislature) against Gray’s proposals.

Gray’s office also did not respond to a request for comment.

In the governor’s race, the candidate who most
[embraced](https://brentbien.com/return-elections-to-the-voter/) Gray’s voting
agenda, Brent Bien, finished a distant third. He was endorsed by the Freedom
Caucus but lost to Eric Barlow, a state senator [who has
clashed](https://www.foxnews.com/politics/cowboy-state-republican-who-mounted-
gubernatorial-bid-isnt-conservative-enough-freedom-caucus-chair-says.amp) with
ultra-conservative lawmakers.

Republican nominees will be favored in November in this deep red state that
Trump won by 46 percentage points in 2024, but even here, Democrats hope to
make inroads this year—and [they’ve
said](https://cowboystatedaily.com/2026/05/28/democrats-now-have-parties-in-
all-23-wyoming-counties-for-the-first-time-in-modern-memory) the unpopular
influence the Freedom Caucus has had on the state could help their candidates.

In the secretary of state race, Democrats last week nominated Bryan McCarty,
an attorney who ran unopposed in the primary. He also rejects the notion that
fraud is a rampant issue that requires new voting restrictions. Of Wyoming's
2025 law requiring proof of citizenship, he told _Bolts_ , “It's a solution in
search of a problem that does not exist.”

Asked about the Freedom Caucus’ proposals to restrict mail voting, he said,
“I'm going to just point out that the president votes by mail.”

McCarty thinks that Short is running a good campaign but that it's important
for voters to reject the party that has enabled Trump, including around voting
issues. “The consequence of a lot of the stuff they are proposing is that it
does and will make it harder for people to vote, and that is very blatantly
the objective of their exercise,” he said. “They want to stymie voting.”

McCarty and Short, who’ll face each other in November, both saved their
sharpest criticism for the man they’re seeking to replace. McCarty blamed Gray
for following Trump’s lead during his four years as Wyoming’s top elections
official, while Short faulted the outgoing secretary of state for undermining
people's confidence in elections.

Short said, “I believe that fomenting distrust in a world full of hyperbole
that's echoed and even amplified by social media was just a ploy to gain
notoriety.”
